sources.news_title: U.S. Senate Passes Temporary Budget Bill to Prevent Shutdown... 'Voter ID Act' Fails
sources.text:
(워싱턴=연합뉴스) 홍정규 특파원 = 미국 연방정부의 일부 기능정지(셧다운)를 피하기 위한 임시예산안(CR·Continuing Resolution)이 미 연방의회 상원을 8일(현지시간) 통과했다.
이날 새벽 상원 본회의에서 가결된 임시예산안은 중간선거 한 달 뒤인 12월 11일까지 연방정부 운영 자금을 현재 수준으로 유지하는 내용이다.
임시예산안이 발효되면 본예산 처리를 위한 시간을 벌게 된다. 본예산이 처리되지 못한 채 9월 말 회계연도가 종료되더라도 셧다운은 피할 수 있는 셈이다.
도널드 트럼프 2기 행정부는 지난해 9월 말까지 본예산 처리에 실패하고 임시예산안도 마련하지 못하면서 셧다운에 돌입, 항공 대란과 보조금 지급 중단 등 혼란을 유발한 끝에 11월 12일 종료된 바 있다. 이는 역대 최장 기간(43일)의 셧다운이었다.
올해 들어서도 트럼프 행정부의 강경 이민정책 등을 이유로 국토안보부가 부분 셧다운에 들어가 76일 만인 지난 4월 30일 종료되기도 했다.
임시예산안이 상원을 통과한 내용대로 확정될지는 불확실하다. 하원에서 별도로 통과한 임시예산안이 상원이 마련한 것과 일부 상충하기 때문이다.
대표적인 게 연방정부의 보조금 집행에 대해 백악관 예산관리국(OMB)이 제동을 걸거나 임의로 변경할 수 없도록 '보조금 승인 절차' 변경을 금지하는 내용이다.
하원 안에는 이 내용이 담기지 않은 반면, 상원은 트럼프 행정부가 각 주(州)나 단체에 지급되는 보조금을 정치적으로 무기화해선 안 된다는 이유로 이 내용을 담았다.
상원의 임시예산안은 트럼프 행정부의 반(反)이민 정책을 집행하는 이민세관단속국(ICE)과 세관국경보호국(CBP)에 대한 자금 지원도 포함하지 않았다.
'트럼프 충성파'인 공화당 소속 마이크 존슨 의장이 주도권을 쥔 하원과, 일부 공화당 의원이 트럼프 대통령과 엇박자를 내는 상원이 임시예산안을 놓고 충돌할 수 있는 셈이다.
상·하원의 '여름 휴회'가 모두 종료되는 9월 중순부터 두 임시예산안을 놓고 절충이 이뤄지지 않으면 셧다운이 현실화할 가능성을 배제할 수 없다.
트럼프 대통령은 자신이 강조해 온 유권자 신분검사 강화 법안(유권자 ID 법안)도 함께 처리돼야 한다고 전날 심야에 공화당 지도부에 전화를 걸어 거듭 촉구했지만, 끝내 관철되지 못했다.
일명 'SAVE 법'으로 불리는 이 법안은 유권자의 신분증 제시와 시민권 증명, 우편투표의 원칙적 금지 등이 골자다.
트럼프 대통령은 60석이 아닌 과반 찬성이 가결 요건인 예산조정절차를 활용, 민주당의 필리버스터(합법적 의사진행 방해)를 무력화해 이 법안을 처리해야 한다는 입장이지만, 공화당 지도부는 의회 관례와 규칙에 어긋난다며 반대한다.
상원 공화당 내 친(親)트럼프 진영을 중심으로 필리버스터 대상이 아닌 예산결의안을 마련, 여기에 이란 전쟁 등에 필요한 국방 예산과 함께 SAVE 법안의 일부를 예산에 영향을 주는 형태로 끼워넣어 통과시키는 1천500억달러의 패키지 예산안이 대안으로 거론되지만, 이번 회기에는 표결에 부쳐지지 않았다.

sources.news_title: Senate passes stopgap funding bill to last through November elections
List of senators who voted against stopgap bill to avert federal shutdown
sources.text:
The Senate passed a short-term funding bill 90-6 early Saturday, keeping the federal government funded through December 11 and pushing the next potential shutdown deadline beyond the November midterm elections.
The measure extends current funding levels after the government's existing funding expires September 30 and includes several provisions negotiated by lawmakers.
The House has already passed a separate continuing resolution that would fund the government through December 4. The two chambers will therefore have to reconcile their different versions before the legislation can be sent to Trump for his signature.
What The Senate Funding Bill Does
The Senate bill is a continuing resolution, meaning it temporarily extends federal government funding rather than establishing full-year fiscal 2027 appropriations.
It generally maintains current funding levels through December 11, giving Congress additional time to negotiate the individual appropriations bills needed to fund the government for the rest of fiscal year 2027.
The legislation also contains several significant exceptions and policy provisions.
One provision sought by Democrats would prevent funds from being transferred to the Border Patrol. Democrats had opposed giving the Trump administration additional flexibility to redirect money toward border security.
The measure also includes language allowing funding adjustments for housing and food assistance programs, as reported by Reuters.
Another provision has become a point of contention among Republicans: the bill delays implementation of a national ban on most intoxicating hemp products by one month.
The legislation also includes a provision backed by Democrats and some Republicans on the Appropriations Committee, as reported by The Hill, that would temporarily block a White House budget office rule giving executive branch political appointees greater authority over the distribution of federal grants.
The proposed rule would require senior political appointees to review grants before they are awarded and determine whether they advance the president's policy priorities.
Democrats have argued that the proposal could politicize the federal grant-making process, while the White House Office of Management and Budget has said the change is intended to improve accountability and prevent taxpayer money from being wasted or misused.
The Six Senators Who Voted Against The Bill
The final vote was 90-6, meaning six senators opposed the Senate's version of the stopgap. The opposition came from three Democrats, one Independent and two Republicans:
Bill Cassidy (R-La.)
Cassidy has served in the Senate since 2015. A physician by profession, he has focused heavily on health care, fiscal policy and government spending during his time in Congress. Before joining the Senate, Cassidy served three terms in the House of Representatives.
Tim Kaine (D-Va.)
Kaine has represented Virginia in the Senate since 2013. He previously served as Virginia's governor and lieutenant governor and was mayor of Richmond. A Democrat, Kaine has been involved in foreign policy, military affairs and economic issues and was Hillary Clinton's running mate in the 2016 presidential election.
Ed Markey (D-Mass.)
Markey has represented Massachusetts in the Senate since 2013, after more than three decades in the House. He is a prominent Democratic voice on climate change, clean energy and technology policy. Markey has also been a leading advocate for stronger regulation of technology companies and protections for consumers.
Rand Paul (R-Ky.)
Paul, a Republican and physician, has represented Kentucky in the Senate since 2011. He is known for his focus on reducing federal spending, limiting government power and addressing the national debt. Paul has frequently opposed large spending packages and has been one of the Senate's more outspoken critics of government borrowing.
Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.)
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, has represented Vermont in the Senate since 2007. Before that, he served in the House and was mayor of Burlington. Sanders is a longtime progressive voice who has campaigned for expanded health care, higher wages, stronger labor protections and increased taxes on wealthy Americans and corporations.
Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.)
Warren has represented Massachusetts in the Senate since 2013. A former Harvard Law School professor and consumer-protection scholar, she has made financial regulation, economic inequality and consumer rights central issues throughout her Senate career. She was also a candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2020.
Newsweek contacted all six senators via online form or email Saturday for comment.
Why The Bill Matters For The Midterm Elections
The Senate bill would extend government funding through December 11, pushing the next potential shutdown deadline past the November 3 midterm elections. Senate Majority Leader John Thune urged lawmakers to reach an agreement before the August recess to avoid a shutdown fight during the campaign season.
The House has passed a separate measure that would fund the government through December 4, leaving lawmakers to resolve the difference before the bill can become law.
What Happens Next
The Senate's vote does not yet avert the possibility of a shutdown.
The House has already approved its own continuing resolution, but that legislation would expire on December 4 rather than December 11. The two chambers must agree on identical legislation before it can be sent to Trump.
If Congress resolves the differences and Trump signs the legislation, federal agencies would remain funded through December 11, preventing a shutdown immediately before the November midterm elections.
The December deadline would then set up another major spending fight after Election Day, when lawmakers would have to agree on full-year fiscal 2027 appropriations or approve another temporary extension.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Trevor Davies

sources.news_title: Senate Kicks the Can Again With Funding Bill That Handcuffs Trump on the Border
sources.text:
Another Saturday, another stopgap bill. The Senate voted 90-6 in the early hours of August 8 to keep the federal government funded through December 11, then bolted for August recess. No real cuts. No permanent fixes. Just another short-term patch so lawmakers can campaign without a shutdown hanging over their heads.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune pushed the measure through before senators scattered to their home states. Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic leadership let it move. The bill maintains current funding levels with a handful of adjustments for programs like WIC and some national security items. It now heads to the House, which already passed its own version last month and returns August 31.
Here is the part that should make conservatives grind their teeth. Democrats extracted two key concessions. The legislation blocks the Trump administration from shifting money to Border Patrol or ICE from other accounts. It also temporarily freezes an Office of Management and Budget rule that would have given political appointees more authority over federal grants.
Read that again. At a time when the southern border remains a national emergency and illegal aliens continue testing every weak point, Senate negotiators agreed to language that limits the president’s ability to move resources to the agencies charged with enforcing the law.
RINO Susan Collins, the Republican chair of the Appropriations Committee, joined Democrats in opposing the grants rule, calling it deeply flawed. The result is a bipartisan deal that preserves the status quo more than it strengthens the executive’s hand.
This is not governing. It is political risk management. Lawmakers remember the messy shutdowns of the past year. Neither party wanted another one weeks before the midterms. So they did what Congress always does: spend now, decide later, and call it responsibility.
The House version lacked these restrictions. The Senate added them. That is the real story. Even with Republicans holding the majority and a Republican in the White House, Democratic demands shaped the final product.
Schumer called it a responsible path forward. Of course he did. Any measure that constrains Trump’s flexibility on immigration enforcement and federal spending priorities is a win for the left.
Scripture is clear about the duty of those who hold the sword. Romans 13:4 describes the ruler as “the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.”
A government that cannot freely deploy resources to secure its borders and protect its people fails that basic test. Kicking the funding can into December does nothing to change the deeper problem of a Congress addicted to short-term patches and allergic to hard choices.
Thune warned Democrats that if they blocked the measure he would turn to reconciliation. They did not block it. They shaped it instead. The bill still needs House approval and the president’s signature before September 30. House Republicans may push back on the grants language and the border restrictions. They should.
America does not need another continuing resolution that treats border security as optional and executive authority as something to be bargained away. It needs lawmakers willing to fund the government in a way that actually serves the nation’s interests rather than the political calendar.
We need cuts. We need the right programs funded and the wrong programs scrapped. We need a real reckoning in Washington DC that addresses the ballooning national debt. Until that happens, these late-night votes will keep coming, and the real work will keep waiting.

sources.news_title: Senate Once Again Kicks Funding Can Down The Road
sources.text:
The Senate passed a continuing resolution (CR) early Saturday to fund the government without addressing the national debt.
The CR would fund the government through Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown ahead of the midterm elections. The funding bill extends current funding levels rather than addressing the national debt, which amounts to approximately $39.8 trillion.
The House passed its own version of a CR on July 21 in a 220 to 205 vote, which would fund the government until Dec. 4.
The Senate voted to invoke cloture on the CR in a 91 to 6 vote, which limited debate so the floor could eventually vote on final passage. Republican Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy, Republican Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul, Democratic Massachusetts Sens. Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine voted against the motion.
The final vote on the CR was 90-6, as South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham voted “present” because it included a death benefit to the heir of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham.
The legislation is a standard stopgap measure that continues current government spending levels, meaning no spending cuts were added. (RELATED: Brouhaha Over Hemp Ban Delay Could Cause Major Funding Bill To Go Up In Smoke)
Paul expressed concern over the national debt in a Friday X post. He referred to a $95 billion reconciliation package that passed the House on July 22 and included no offsets.
“Today we will vote on 2 budgets: One spends $100 billion MORE and is not offset by cuts. Pure debt. 
The other budget actually cuts spending by $400 billion dollars! Call your legislators and demand they vote for NO MORE DEBT!” Paul said. 
Today we will vote on 2 budgets: 
One spends $100 billion MORE and is not offset by cuts. Pure debt. 
The other budget actually cuts spending by $400 billion dollars! 
Call your legislators and demand they vote for NO MORE DEBT!
Lawmakers disagreed on a provision that would delay banning hemp THC products. Republican North Carolina Sen. Ted Budd introduced an amendment to strip a provision that would delay a ban on hemp scheduled for November until Dec. 11, which is expected to pass.
The White House requested a delay, arguing the brief delay would allow lawmakers and industry stakeholders to negotiate a reasonable federal regulatory system rather than abruptly shutting down a multi-billion dollar industry. Republican senators confronted White House legislative affairs chief James Braid over the hemp issue during a Senate GOP lunch, Punchbowl reported.
The Senate had planned to vote on the CR Friday before leaving for the August recess. The Senate Appropriations Committee advanced it out of the committee in a Monday vote.

sources.news_title: Senate passes deal to avoid government shutdown before recess, but not Trump's voting bill
sources.text:
Senate adjourns after passing deal to avert government shutdown, but without advancing voting bill
Senators headed for the exits in the predawn hours Saturday, ending for now a standoff over President Donald Trump's demands that they stay in session to pass a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill before the summer recess.
While they wrapped up many key priorities in the overnight votes, advancing Trump's SAVE America Act was not among them.
Instead, Republican senators who had brought the chamber to a standstill spoke to Trump late in the evening about an alternative plan: They would try again to approve elements of the voting bill as part of a broader GOP budget package to fund the Iran war and replenish the Pentagon when they return to work in September.
“Obviously, with the president at his direction, this is what he wants to do,” said Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, the GOP budget committee chairman, flanked by Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah, and Rick Scott, R-Fla., after their phone call with the president.
Trump had poked and prodded Senate Majority Leader John Thune for weeks to pass the SAVE America Act, a bill that does not have enough support from the Republicans who hold majority power, let alone the Democrats whose votes would be needed to advance it in the Senate.
The president has gone so far as to insist the Senate abandon its filibuster rules to jam the SAVE America Act past the 60-vote threshold that is typically needed to advance legislation in the chamber — something Thune and most senators have no interest in doing.
“John’s trying. He’s trying hard. I really believe that. But if he doesn’t get there, it would be unfortunate,” Trump said in an interview with Punchbowl News that posted Friday.
Trump's pressure couldn't overcome Thune's reality
Thune himself has worked to carefully balance the often unusual demands of the president with the political reality of his slim GOP majority. Republicans are down one vote with the prolonged absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, the former leader, who said this week he was released from a rehabilitation center and is recovering at home.
“I think everybody’s, for the most part, on the same page,” Thune, R-S.D., said about the trio's call with Trump, adding that eventually the Senate would have to tackle another budget bill.
During a daylong session that dragged for nearly 20 hours, Thune successfully powered through a lengthy list of other Trump priorities. Senators confirmed the president's pick of Todd Blanche as the attorney general, passed a sweeping Russian sanctions package to aid Ukraine, and approved a bipartisan package to fund the government into December in an early step toward avoiding a government shutdown.
The Republicans also tried to push forward a slimmer voting bill that would require people to show IDs before casting ballots for federal elections. It failed to advance, largely on a party-line vote with Democrats opposed.
But the failure to make progress on the SAVE America Act had erupted as an online crusade for Trump's allies in Congress, amplified by activists urging them on.
Led by Lee, a growing group of senators was refusing to adjourn for the summer break without passing Trump's priority voting bill.
At dinnertime, Thune gathered all the Republican senators for a meeting as the standoff deepened at the Capitol. There was no immediate way forward for the SAVE America Act or the broader budget bill. Thune encouraged the trio of senators to talk to the president, which they did, before regrouping back at Thune's office.
"We had about a two-hour conference meeting trying to figure out, you know, what we need to do to, to come to an agreement, to accomplish what the president wanted,” Johnson said. “Then we had discussion with the president, he agrees.”
Lee acknowledged he was disappointed by the outcome, but said he understood the political reality of the situation.
“We are not in a position right now where we have the wherewithal to pass it,” Lee told reporters at the Capitol, after the three senators emerged from Thune's office following their call with Trump.
Near daybreak, when the Senate did call for the vote to adjourn, Lee and others objected with hearty nos.
On the simple voice vote, the ayes had it, and the motion to adjourn was adopted.

sources.news_title: US Senate averts shutdown before Midterms, curbs Trump on Border Patrol funds, delays Hemp ban
sources.text:
The US Senate on Saturday (8 August) passed a stopgap spending bill to avert a government shutdown at the end of September, in a bipartisan effort to head off a major spending skirmish before the midterm elections.
Senators approved the stopgap measure by 90 votes to six, with one member voting present, extending current funding levels well past the original 30 September deadline. The bill also blocks the Trump administration from shifting funds toward Border Patrol, a restriction Democrats had made a condition of their support.
Whether the agreement, hashed out among senators, can clear the House remains uncertain, though members there are said to share the same reluctance to risk a shutdown before November.
What stood out as much as the vote itself was its timing. Congress has grown accustomed to funding fights that go down to the wire, but this bill passed with more than a month to spare. Two shutdowns within the past year, combined with the political pressure of an approaching election, appear to have concentrated minds early.
Susan Collins, the Maine Republican who chairs the Appropriations Committee, framed the vote as a lesson learned. "After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us," she said.
For Democrats, the bill's restriction on redirecting money to Border Patrol carried particular weight. The issue sat at the centre of the previous shutdown, and its inclusion this time was treated by the party as a meaningful concession.
Patty Murray of Washington, the senior Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, described the bill as buying time for tougher negotiations ahead. "This is an important step forward to prevent a shutdown no one wants and provide the runway we need to negotiate funding bills in the months ahead as we fight to rein in Trump's corruption and make life more affordable for families back home," she said.
The smoothest part of the process was not the funding itself but a late addition concerning intoxicating hemp products, inserted into the bill at Trump's request. The provision delays by a month a ban on such products that Congress had approved and Trump had signed into law the previous year, a ban that was due to take effect in November.
Republican leaders added the delay to the stopgap legislation at the White House's urging, a decision that angered some within their own party. A group of Republican senators attempted to strip the provision out entirely.
Ted Budd of North Carolina argued forcefully for letting the original ban proceed on schedule, pointing to the packaging and branding used by companies selling the products. "It's no accident that these products are made to look exactly like something that a kid would want," he said, warning that the hemp industry was working "to permanently entrench their intoxicating products into the machinery of government."
The delay stands to benefit the son-in-law of Susie Wiles, Trump's chief of staff, who runs companies that distribute and sell intoxicating hemp-derived gummies and vapes marketed under names such as "Trainwreck" and "Blueberry Cookies."
The White House defended the one-month reprieve as a measure that would support veterans and patients managing pain, rather than a concession to industry. That argument prevailed. Senators voted 61 to 32 to reject the effort to remove the delay, allowing it to remain in the final bill.

sources.news_title: Senate passes bill to fund government in bid to avert shutdown ahead of midterm elections
sources.text:
The Senate passed a bill on Saturday that would extend government funding to December 11 in a bid to avert a shutdown ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
The chamber moved to tackle the funding deadline over a month in advance of the September 30 deadline. It’s not yet clear though if lawmakers will manage to stave off a funding fight next month.
The bill passed by the Senate would next have to be taken up by the House, where its fate is uncertain as that chamber has already passed an alternative measure.
The Senate measure differs from a funding extension passed by the House in several ways, including a lack of funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, which have already been funded through the end of President Donald Trump’s term, and a temporary block on a proposed administration rule that critics warn would further politicize federal grants.
Senate leaves for August recess
The Senate vote to pass the funding bill came in the early hours of Saturday morning, as senators attempted to wrap up a number of legislative items before departing Washington to return to their home states for the August recess.
Ultimately, in addition to adopting the measure to extend government funding into December, the Senate also confirmed acting attorney general Todd Blanche as the permanent head of the Department of Justice, and, separately, rejected a voter ID measure.
However, Senate Republicans chose to delay for now a vote on their budget resolution, which was meant to be a party-line package containing defense funding and parts of a controversial elections bill, after President Donald Trump called into a late meeting at the Capitol with several senators on Friday night to discuss their options, those senators said.
Trump had demanded that the Senate pass the budget resolution before leaving town for their recess, and GOP Sen. Mike Lee had said he would object to any effort to speed up consideration and leave if the budget resolution did not pass. Both Trump and Lee have been pushing for the president’s elections package, known as the “SAVE America Act,” for months.
However, Sen. Ron Johnson, who chairs the Senate budget committee, told reporters that during a meeting in Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s office on Friday night, the president called in and there was unanimous agreement that the GOP senators will go back to the drawing board for a “better” budget resolution, including more defense funding, that they can pursue when they return in September, rather than face a failed vote to advance a budget resolution this week.
Republican leadership had also hoped to at least take a preliminary procedural vote on a bill focused on regulating name, image, and likeness deals in college sports, but senators were unable to reach a deal on the package.

sources.text:
Washington — The Senate voted Saturday to pass a continuing resolution that would keep federal agencies funded through Dec. 11, sending the stopgap spending bill to the House as Congress tries to avert a government shutdown before this fall’s midterm elections.
The measure cleared the Senate in a lopsided 90-6 vote. It would extend government funding at current levels, with several exceptions, for six weeks beyond the Sept. 30 close of the fiscal year. The bill now heads to the House, where lawmakers have been moving along a different track.
Before departing Washington for its August recess, the House passed its own continuing resolution to fund the government into December. That GOP-led proposal, however, drew broad opposition from Democrats.
In the Senate, where most legislation needs 60 votes to advance, Republican leaders opted for a bipartisan strategy on the short-term funding extension, recognizing that Democratic support would be necessary.
The Senate’s top Republican and Democratic appropriators announced Sunday that they had reached a deal on the temporary spending bill. Democrats pointed to several provisions they viewed as victories, including language closing a loophole that had prevented the administration from shifting funds to Border Patrol after Democrats earlier this year declined to fund immigration enforcement agencies. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, the Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, praised the agreement for steering clear of “any poison pills.” Democrats had pushed for additional measures that might have jeopardized the bill’s chances.

The legislation includes a temporary block on political appointees in the administration carrying out a proposed rule involving federal grants. Democrats have warned the rule would let the administration cancel grants and “take even more federal funding hostage,” and they have pressed for a permanent prohibition. Even a temporary restriction, though, could cost the bill some Republican support.

Senate passes bill to avert government shutdown before midterm elections

sources.text:
The Senate advanced its solution to avert a government shutdown on Saturday, capping off several months of hand-wringing that, if given the chance, Senate Democrats would use a shutdown to score political points in November.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his caucus relented, and stayed true to the bargain they struck with Republicans to keep the government funded well past Election Night and into early December.
The about-face, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital, appeared to be a political calculation on Schumer and Democrats’ part.
SCHUMER CLAIMS VICTORY AS SENATE MOVES TO AVERT SHUTDOWN; GOP SAYS HE GOT PLAYED
"I think they didn't want to spend the next, well … three months defending attacks from Republicans about wanting to shut the government down," Thune said.
"I mean, I think there was a narrative starting to build out there based on what's happened the last 12 months, which I think, they probably — you know, these guys are political animals," Thune continued. "I'm assuming those guys are polling all the time."
DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE
And Schumer claimed victory over the process, arguing that Democrats "for months" wanted to keep the government open, and had scored key concessions from the Trump administration on an ensuing rule change to federal grants in the bipartisan continuing resolution (CR).
"We want to reach across the aisle and hammer out a budget that delivers for the American people," Schumer said on the Senate floor. "Today, [this] CR gives us the breathing room necessary to work out a budget that helps make life more affordable to working families and reigns in Trump's rampant chaos, his rampant corruption."
However, Republicans have been messaging for months that congressional Democrats wouldn’t bat an eye at shutting the government down again. In the Senate, efforts have been made to inflict pain on lawmakers should another shutdown happen, like agreeing to forego their paychecks in the event of a closure.
SENATE TAKES MAJOR FIRST STEP TO PREVENT FUTURE SHUTDOWNS WITH PAINFUL ACCOUNTABILITY PLAY
That follows two government shutdowns that etched their way into the record books at 43 and 76 days, respectively, but the political winds didn’t appear to be in Democrats’ favor this go-round, the top Senate Republican said.
"And I think they see an issue set that works for them going into the fall election, and I think they view a government shutdown or the prospect of not funding the government as creating uncertainty that perhaps didn't help their chances," Thune said.

WASHINGTON — The Senate voted 90-6 early Saturday to pass a short-term funding bill to remove the threat of a government shutdown before the midterm elections.
The legislation, advanced in a late-night session that stretched into the early hours, would keep federal funds flowing through Dec. 11 at existing levels to give time to negotiate a full-year deal.
It was negotiated by the two parties and includes some modest add-ons, including a provision demanded by Democrats aimed at preventing President Donald Trump from blocking federal grants to blue states for political reasons.
It also includes some adjustments to preserve the SNAP and WIC food programs, in addition to disaster relief and national security measures.

If so, it would prevent the sort of brinkmanship that has become common in Congress ahead of the fall deadline. There is a broad anti-incumbency mood in the electorate that has afflicted both parties during this primary season, and neither side wanted to risk a shutdown that could carry treacherous political consequences just before Election Day on Nov. 3.
The House passed a different short-term government funding bill last month before leaving for the August recess. After wrapping up some lingering business, the Senate also adjourned for the month just before 5 a.m. ET. Senators are set to return on Sept. 14.

sources.news_title: Funding patch passes Senate to head off fall shutdown
sources.text:
Funding patch passes Senate to head off fall shutdown
But the bill still requires a vote in the House, which won't be back until September
The Senate easily passed a bipartisan continuing resolution early Saturday morning, likely easing the traditional September rush to head off a partial government shutdown in October.
On a lopsided vote of 90-6, the Senate passed a measure that would extend current funding through Dec. 11, giving lawmakers about 10 extra weeks to complete full-year appropriations bills for fiscal 2027.
But the bill still requires a vote in the House, which won’t be back in session until the first week of September. The House had passed a more bare-bones funding extension last month without many of the “anomalies,” or deviations in current spending, requested by the Trump administration.
The Senate bill passed only after a contentious, days-long dispute over the sale of some THC-infused hemp products, which held up a timing agreement for days. The bill included a provision, sought by the administration, to delay a ban on the sale of those products that is set to take effect Nov. 12.
Sens. Ted Budd, R-N.C., and Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., demanded a vote on their amendment to strip out that provision in exchange for their support to speed up the process. The Senate tabled that amendment on a 61-32 vote, thereby allowing for a roughly four-week delay of the ban, as the White House sought.
While passage of the bipartisan stopgap measure was in little doubt, bringing it to the finish line took days of negotiating as leaders struggled to reach a timing agreement by unanimous consent to speed up consideration of the bill along with other legislation they sought to pass before the Senate left town for its long August recess. That agreement also cleared the way for the confirmation of Todd Blanche to be attorney general.
Barring unexpected events, the funding patch is not likely to have much difficulty getting across the House floor after the widely bipartisan vote in the Senate. Lawmakers are eager to return to the campaign trail in October ahead of the November midterm elections.
But there is still a chance that the House could try to amend the Senate bill if any new concerns crop up over the long August recess that lawmakers want to address in a must-pass vehicle like the continuing resolution.
Unlike the House measure, the Senate bill includes a few notable curbs on the administration’s authority.
In a contentious provision that had held up a deal last month, the bill would block, until Dec. 11, a federal rule requiring grants to be approved by senior political appointees — a proposal that triggered an avalanche of public criticism.
Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrats oppose the rule, arguing that it will slow the flow of federal funds and insert more political influence into the process.
But supporters of the administration are poised to fight against any future delays or an outright ban on the rule.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said earlier this week that there would be a “big fight” over the issue in December, though he said White House budget director Russ Vought told him a delay now was acceptable since the rule would not be ready to be finalized before December anyway.
In another restriction on White House authority, Democrats said the bill would close a “loophole” that would have allowed the administration to transfer further funding to the Border Patrol.
House Democrats overwhelmingly rejected the recent funding patch passed mostly by Republicans in the House, partly because it lacked an explicit prohibition against new Border Patrol funding, as Democrats seek to impose new curbs on immigration agents.
Senate Democrats also succeeded in excluding from the bill a White House request for $1 billion to begin building “Trump-class” battleships, though the measure includes other administration requests to accelerate funding for Navy shipbuilding programs.
The bill also includes a basic extension of funding for the nation’s surface transportation programs through Dec. 11 as work on a full reauthorization continues.
And the Senate bill would extend for two years economic pacts with sub-Saharan African countries and with Haiti, while allowing for quicker spending for food assistance and disaster relief.
Paul M. Krawzak contributed to this report.
